prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Management by Trajectory (MBT), a far-term Concept of Operations (ConOps) guiding research, implements Trajectory Based Operations (TBO) consistently with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance, resembling four-dimensional (4D) contracts. National Airspace System (NAS), Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), airspace users, aircraft, pilots, air traffic controllers, traffic managers, stakeholders, and ground/aircraft automation participate.
MBT covers all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft, including commercial aviation, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, and on-demand air transportation vehicles. FAA/users negotiate and assign closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current state to destination, respecting user goals and all applicable constraints. Aircraft must follow assigned trajectories/constraints; pilots/controllers use compliance automation, with equipped aircraft substantially responsible. Tolerances reflect flight performance/situational need.
NAS Constraint Service publishes common static/dynamic NAS constraints to stakeholders. Traffic management automation identifies flights affected by each traffic management initiative (TMI), translating it into flight-specific trajectory constraints. Constraints map to NAS constraints. Publish every trajectory change to relevant users, aircraft, and FAA automation for synchronized predictions. Aircraft share predicted 4DTs (intent data) with stakeholders and update changed intent.
Traffic managers amend trajectories as events evolve. Consider downstream effects in every decision, including tactical actions; intervene proactively. Earlier conflict detection enables adding/modifying assigned constraints. Minimize open trajectories (tactical vectoring with unknown intent) through closed tactical modifications and improved predictability.
Digital air-ground communications deliver cockpit 4DTs for Flight Management System (FMS) loading/execution. Broadband communications and electronic flight bag (EFB) applications enable crew negotiation. Negotiating controller subsumes D-side controller responsibilities; with traffic management coordinators (TMCs), proactively avoids conflicts and achieves traffic flow management (TFM) objectives. Automation coordinates multisector changes.
Far-term targets NAS/most aircraft supporting Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2) capabilities. Near-term feasibility is explored. Quantified time-based performance complements Performance Based Navigation (PBN); time of arrival control (TOAC) certification thresholds risk mixed equipage/separate concepts and unacceptable risk.

New part:
U0058: First, the near-term concept is constrained by the current NAS and currently planned changes to the NAS (i.e., changes that the FAA plans and are documented within the NAS Enterprise Architecture [EA] evolution within the NextGen timeframe), while the far-term concept may make assumptions about future enabling changes.
U0059: Second, while the far-term concept encompasses the entirety of air traffic control (ATC) within the NAS, in the near-term a more limited set of TBO operations may be feasible and beneficial. 1.5 Assumptions This section summarizes key assumptions about the near-term and far-term environments in which MBT would operate. 1.5.1 Assumptions about the Near-Term MBT Environment  Air traffic controllers will still be responsible for separation management and conflict avoidance; self-separation of IFR aircraft will not be the norm in the far-term MBT environment.  Air vehicle capabilities and equipage will be consistent with the current progression of safety and performance standards.  The capabilities of highly equipped aircraft will not change.
U0060: For example, aircraft FMS that include Required Time of Arrival (RTA) functionality will remain limited to a single active RTA constraint at a time.
U0061: Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) with route clearances and trajectory intent output will be standard services supported by avionics.  MBT will slowly seep into NAS operations; there will not be a step change in procedures.
U0062: This will allow equipped aircraft to experience some benefit while operating among unequipped aircraft, and allow controllers with different perspectives on changing technologies and procedures to adapt to MBT at different paces.  MBT tools will be introduced incrementally through upgrades to existing automation platforms and extensions to the information shared via System Wide Information Management (SWIM).
U0063: Adoption of MBT will be varied around the NAS with some facilities and controllers more willing and able to adopt new capabilities than others.
U0064: Benefits will initially be slow to accumulate as controllers become more comfortable with the technologies.
U0065: Experience will allow the tools to be refined to improve performance and increase user acceptance.
U0066: Eventually, a critical mass of usage will be reached, resulting in increased usage and benefits.  Adoption of supporting technologies by airspace users will continue at its current pace.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
